reviewer.name: Independent Jinshu 119 structured reviewer; accepted English proofs reused

proposals.before: Yao Hong, courtesy Yuanzi, was Yao Xing's firstborn.
proposals.after: Yao Hong, whose courtesy name was Yuanzi, was Yao Xing’s eldest son.
proposals.reason: 長子 identifies the eldest son. “Firstborn” omits that he is a son and could imply that he is the eldest of all the children.

proposals.before: He was dutiful, gentle, and kind, but had no talent for governing a realm, and he was often ill—so Yao Xing long hesitated before naming him heir.
proposals.after: He was dutiful to his parents, affectionate toward his brothers, generous and mild. But he lacked the ability to govern and was often ill, so Yao Xing hesitated over making him heir.
proposals.reason: 孝友 includes devotion to siblings as well as filial piety.

proposals.before: He was filial, friendly, generous, and mild, yet lacked the ability to order the age, and moreover often fell ill; Xing was about to make him heir yet hesitated.
proposals.after: He was filial, affectionate toward his brothers, generous and mild, yet lacked the ability to govern the realm and was often ill. Xing intended to make him heir but hesitated.
proposals.reason: 友 in 孝友 denotes affection toward siblings.

proposals.before: Wang Shang, Duan Zhang, and Fu Yunwen tutored him in the classics; Hu Yizhou and Xiahou Zhi kept him company over belles-lettres.
proposals.after: Wang Shang, a master of writing, Duan Zhang, a gentleman of the Yellow Gates, and Fu Yunwen, a gentleman of the Department of State Affairs, tutored him in the classics. Hu Yizhou and Xiahou Zhi joined him for literary gatherings.
proposals.reason: Restore the distinct offices of all three Confucian tutors.

proposals.before: Director Wang Shang, Gentleman of the Yellow Gates Duan Zhang, and Director Gentleman Fu Yunwen attended lectures with Confucian learning; Hu Yizhou and Xiahou Zhi gathered in literary companionship.
proposals.after: Master of Writing Wang Shang, Gentleman of the Yellow Gates Duan Zhang, and gentleman of the Department of State Affairs Fu Yunwen attended him as lecturers on Confucian learning. Hu Yizhou and Xiahou Zhi joined him in literary gatherings.
proposals.reason: 侍講 describes lecturing to Hong, not attending lectures as pupils; 尚書郎 is a departmental gentleman.

proposals.before: Director Wang Min and aide Guo Bo thought the laws too soft and pressed for crackdowns. Yao Hong replied: "Humiliate people and you breed defiance.
proposals.after: Wang Min, a master of writing, and Guo Bo, the right assistant director, thought the administration of punishments too lenient and proposed stricter regulations. Yao Hong replied, “Humiliate people and you breed defiance.
proposals.reason: 右丞 specifies Guo’s office and 以刑政過寬 covers punishments and governance.

proposals.before: You help run the court—widen the path of mercy, not the jailer's whip; harshness is no way to steady ruler and people."
proposals.after: You gentlemen help guide the court and make its principles of government known. If you neglect humanity and clemency and seek only strict laws and cruel punishments, how can you keep the ruler secure and govern his subjects?”
proposals.reason: The officials’ responsibility for exemplifying government policy and Hong’s rhetorical question about ruling above and below have been compressed away.

proposals.before: After that, every prince who met a tutor bowed as he had done.
proposals.after: After that, dukes and marquises all bowed when they met their tutors.
proposals.reason: 公侯 identifies dukes and marquises.

proposals.before: Yao Hong sent Peng Bailang with palace guards from the heir's residence; Liu Jue was executed and the rest pardoned.
proposals.after: Yao Hong sent Peng Bailang, the General Who Guards the Army, to lead the Eastern Palace guards against Liu Jue. Jue was beheaded and the remaining rebels pardoned.
proposals.reason: Restore Peng’s military title and his commission to attack Jue.

proposals.before: His generals said: "Your victory was swift—publish a victory notice and show the heads to steady the realm."
proposals.after: All the generals urged Hong, “Your Highness devised your plans with lightning speed and swept away the vile rebels. You should issue an open dispatch reporting the victory and claiming a greater number of enemy heads, to reassure people far and near.”
proposals.reason: 廣其首級 concerns the number of heads claimed in the report. Only Jue had been beheaded in the preceding unit. The generals also praise Hong’s swift planning.

proposals.before: The generals all urged Hong, saying, "Your Highness's divine calculations strike like lightning; you have swept away the vile rebels—it is fitting to issue a public bulletin reporting it, broadly display their heads, to comfort feeling far and near."
proposals.after: All the generals urged Hong, “Your Highness devised your plans with lightning speed and swept away the vile rebels. You should issue an open dispatch reporting the victory and claiming a greater number of enemy heads, to reassure people far and near.”
proposals.reason: 廣其首級 concerns the number of heads claimed in the report. Only Jue had been beheaded in the preceding unit. The generals also praise Hong’s swift planning.

proposals.before: I mishandled the pacification and fed rebellion—I should blame myself, not strut and deepen my fault."
proposals.after: I failed to strike the right balance in pacifying and defending the people, and so encouraged the rebels. I ought now to take the blame, reproach myself and acknowledge my guilt before the ranks. How dare I boast extravagantly and make my fault still greater?”
proposals.reason: The sentence connects failures of pacification and defense to the rise of rebellion and adds 歸罪行間 after Hong takes personal responsibility. Preserve the military setting without shifting the blame onto his subordinates.

proposals.before: I failed in pacification and control, thereby growing traitorous bandits; I ought to take blame on myself and assign guilt among the ranks—how dare I overmuch boast and swagger, thereby adding to the burden of fault!"
proposals.after: I failed to strike the right balance in pacifying and defending the people, and so encouraged the rebels. I ought now to take the blame, reproach myself and acknowledge my guilt before the ranks. How dare I boast extravagantly and make my fault still greater?”
proposals.reason: The sentence connects failures of pacification and defense to the rise of rebellion and adds 歸罪行間 after Hong takes personal responsibility. Preserve the military setting without shifting the blame onto his subordinates.

proposals.before: Wei Hua told Murong Zhu: "The crown prince's humility is the dynasty's luck."
proposals.after: Hearing of this, Wei Hua, the right vice-director, told Murong Zhu, governor of Henan, “The crown prince truly is respectful and kind. That is a blessing for the state.”
proposals.reason: Both offices, Hua hearing the incident, and 惠 as kindness in addition to respectful humility are explicit.

proposals.before: His brother Yao Bi plotted to supplant him, yet Yao Hong treated him with unchanged kindness and never showed resentment.
proposals.after: His younger brother Yao Bi plotted to supplant him, yet Yao Hong treated him with unchanged kindness and never showed resentment.
proposals.reason: 弟 specifies a younger brother.

proposals.before: Yao Shao backed Yao Bi, but Yao Hong still trusted him as kin and showed no distrust.
proposals.after: Yao Shao repeatedly supported Bi, yet Hong trusted and honored Shao wholeheartedly and bore him no suspicion on that account.
proposals.reason: 宗事 entails deference or honoring Shao; 嫌 means Hong harbored no suspicion against him on this account.

proposals.before: Yao Shao often acted as wings for Bi; Hong also gave him whole-hearted clan duty and did not take it as suspicion.
proposals.after: Yao Shao repeatedly supported Bi, yet Hong trusted and honored Shao wholeheartedly and bore him no suspicion on that account.
proposals.reason: 宗事 entails deference or honoring Shao; 嫌 means Hong harbored no suspicion against him on this account.

proposals.before: Once Yao Hong took the throne he gave Yao Shao real command; Shao repaid him with loyalty unto death.
proposals.after: When Yao Hong claimed the imperial throne, he entrusted Yao Shao with military command. Moved by this, Shao pledged himself to Hong and remained loyal to the end.
proposals.reason: 僭 conveys the narrator’s view of Hong’s imperial claim, and 感 gives Shao’s response to Hong’s trust.

proposals.before: Yao Yin, Yin Yuan, and their fellow plotters were put to death.
proposals.after: Yao Yin, Duke of Nanyang, Grand General Yin Yuan and others plotted rebellion. Yao Hong put them all to death.
proposals.reason: Restore both offices, the plot to rebel and Hong as the executor.

proposals.before: Yao Hong announced the death, and in the twelfth year of Yixi claimed the throne, declared a general amnesty short of capital crimes, adopted the era Yonghe, and mourned in a hut beside the council hall.
proposals.after: Yao Hong announced the mourning. In the twelfth year of Yixi he claimed the imperial throne, issued a general pardon extending even to those condemned to death, changed the era name to Yonghe and took up quarters in a mourning hut at the council hall.
proposals.reason: 殊死已下 includes prisoners sentenced to death and those with lesser sentences. Both fields reverse that scope.

proposals.before: Hong issued mourning; in the twelfth year of Yixi he presumptuously assumed the imperial seat, greatly pardoned all short of capital crime, changed the era to Yonghe, and lodged in a mourning hut at the consultation hall.
proposals.after: Yao Hong announced the mourning. In the twelfth year of Yixi he claimed the imperial throne, issued a general pardon extending even to those condemned to death, changed the era name to Yonghe and took up quarters in a mourning hut at the council hall.
proposals.reason: 殊死已下 includes prisoners sentenced to death and those with lesser sentences. Both fields reverse that scope.

proposals.before: After the funeral he took the reins himself, promoted every official a grade, and invited blunt counsel on what helped or hurt the state.
proposals.after: After the burial Hong took charge of government himself and promoted every official at court and in the provinces by one rank. He ordered civil and military officers alike to speak freely about policies unsuited to the times and measures that would bring honor and benefit to the dynasty, holding nothing back.
proposals.reason: Restore civil and military officials, the policy question, benefit to the ancestral dynasty and injunction to speak without reserve.

proposals.before: Their chief Dang Rong then bolted for home; Yao Hong sent Yao Zan against him.
proposals.after: The Qiang chief Dang Rong then led his followers in revolt and set out for home. Yao Hong sent Pacifying General Yao Zan to attack him.
proposals.reason: The chief leads his following in revolt, and Yao Zan bears the Pacifying Army title.

proposals.before: Dang Rong yielded; Yao Hong moved the head families to Chang'an and let the rest go home to Li-run.
proposals.after: Dang Rong surrendered. Yao Hong moved several hundred of the leading households to Chang’an and sent the rest back to Lirun.
proposals.reason: 數百戶 gives a specific approximate count.

proposals.before: Mao Yong of Beidi seized the Zhao stockade in revolt; Yao Shao captured him.
proposals.after: Mao Yong, governor of Beidi, occupied the Zhao clan’s stockade in revolt against Yao Hong. Yao Shao attacked and captured him.
proposals.reason: 太守 makes Mao governor of Beidi, and he revolted against Hong.

proposals.before: Adviser Wei Zong, a troublemaker, told Yao Xuan: "The new ruler lacks prestige; Helian Bobo is too strong—the capital's troubles are not over.
proposals.after: After the troops had set out, Yao Xuan’s adviser Wei Zong, a deceitful flatterer who delighted in disorder, urged him, “The ruler has only just taken the throne, and his authority is not yet established. Helian Bobo is powerful, and his incursions are sure to cause great harm. Our court’s troubles cannot yet be put to rest.
proposals.reason: Restore the troops’ departure, Zong’s deceit and flattery, the predicted invasive harm and the threat to the court.

proposals.before: You hold the western shield—think hard.
proposals.after: Your Highness has the duty of protecting the ruling house. You should consider this carefully.
proposals.reason: 維城 depicts the prince’s duty as a bulwark of the state, without a western direction.

proposals.before: Xingwang is a natural fortress commanding three approaches—seize it in earnest and you secure the west and maybe build a power base."
proposals.after: Xingwang is naturally defensible and commands the approaches from three directions. If you occupy it and govern the people there with an open mind, you can secure your position as a bulwark of the dynasty and even lay the foundations of a hegemon’s or a king’s rule.”
proposals.reason: Recover willing and open-minded governance, the dynastic bulwark and the prospect of hegemonic or royal power.

proposals.before: Yao Xuan marched thirty-eight thousand households south from Li-run to fortify Xingwang.
proposals.after: Yao Xuan abandoned Lirun and led thirty-eight thousand households south to hold Xingwang.
proposals.reason: 棄李閏 is abandonment of the garrison; 保 is holding the refuge at Xingwang.

proposals.before: When Yao Xuan left, the Qiang seized Li-run; Yao Shao smashed them.
proposals.after: Once Yao Xuan had moved south, the Qiang groups occupied Lirun in revolt. Yao Shao advanced against them and defeated them.
proposals.reason: 以叛 is an explicit revolt.

proposals.before: Yao Xuan surrendered to Yao Shao, who killed him in fury.
proposals.after: Yao Xuan went to Yao Shao to acknowledge his guilt. Shao killed him in anger.
proposals.reason: 歸罪 identifies Xuan’s acknowledgment of fault.

proposals.before: Earlier Yao Hong had sent Yao Fosheng to recall Yao Xuan; Fosheng instead backed the defection.
proposals.after: Earlier, when Yao Xuan was at Xingwang, Yao Hong had sent Yao Fosheng to reason with him. Fosheng ended up supporting Xuan’s plan.
proposals.reason: Restore the location and avoid supplying a specific recall order or calling Xuan’s plan a defection.

proposals.before: He decreed pensions and perpetual exemptions for families of soldiers who died in royal service.
proposals.after: Yao Hong decreed that soldiers who died in royal service should receive posthumous titles and their families should enjoy perpetual exemption from levies.
proposals.reason: 贈以爵位 is the posthumous award of titles, not a pension for surviving relatives.

proposals.before: Yao Zan objected to raising sixteen household officers to noble rank: "The heir's staff owes loyalty by duty—they have done nothing spectacular yet."
proposals.after: Hong proposed making sixteen palace officers viscounts or barons. Yao Zan objected, “Surely the crown prince’s civil and military officers owe him loyalty as a matter of duty. They have shown no conspicuous merit. Why grant them so many fiefs?”
proposals.reason: Restore Hong’s intention, the two noble ranks, the civil and military staff, and Zan’s question about the extensive grants.

proposals.before: He was about to enfeoff sixteen palace officials as fifth-rank barons and viscounts; Yao Zan remonstrated, saying, "Eastern-palace civil and military naturally ought to have the loyalty of guarding unto death—they have not yet had blazing manifest merit; how can they receive so many enfeoffments?"
proposals.after: He was about to enfeoff sixteen palace officials as viscounts and barons in the five grades of nobility. Yao Zan remonstrated, “The Eastern Palace’s civil and military officers naturally owe it faithful loyalty. They have yet to show conspicuous merit. Why should they receive so many grants of fiefs?”
proposals.reason: 五等 is the five-grade system, not an ordinal shared by the fourth and fifth grades; 守忠 does not specify death.

proposals.before: Yao Hong replied: "Titles exist to reward future service and mark true virtue.
proposals.after: Yao Hong replied, “The court holds out titles to admonish and encourage those who will render service and to give public recognition to outstanding virtue.
proposals.reason: 懲勸 expresses both admonition and encouragement of future service.

proposals.before: I share every grief with my household staff—how could I hoard favors for myself alone?"
proposals.after: I, Yuanzi, have seen my house struck by misfortune. My palace officers shared all these troubles with me. Could I enjoy the good fortune alone without feeling ashamed?”
proposals.reason: 遭家不造 specifies Hong’s family calamity, and Yuanzi is Hong’s self-designation.

proposals.before: Yao Shao urged delay: "Reward them, yes, but wait until spring as the ancients would."
proposals.after: Yao Shao stepped forward. “Your Majesty remembers to reward virtue, and you are right to grant them fiefs. In antiquity people treated such matters with reverence, timing the appointments for the beginning of the year. You could wait until next spring and then deliberate.”
proposals.reason: Restore Shao’s expressed approval of repaying virtue, the ancient practice of attending to the beginning, and his proposal to deliberate next spring.

proposals.before: Tens of thousands of Hu households in Bing, Dingyang, and Ercheng rose against Yao Hong, entered Pingyang, attacked Liyi Yao Chengdu at the Xiongnu fort, raised the Xiongnu Cao Hong as great shanyu, and wherever they went ravaged and plundered.
proposals.after: Several tens of thousands of Hu households from Bingzhou, Dingyang and Ercheng rebelled against Hong. They entered Pingyang, attacked General Yao Chengdu, who held the title Liyi, at the Xiongnu fort, and proclaimed Cao Hong of the Xiongnu grand shanyu. Everywhere they went they ravaged and plundered.
proposals.reason: 立義 is an abbreviated general’s title, and 落 counts tribal households or encampments, not tens of thousands of settlements.

proposals.before: Several tens of thousands of settlements of Hu in Bingzhou, Dingyang, and Ercheng rebelled against Hong and entered Pingyang, attacked Liyi Yao Chengdu at the Xiongnu fort, pushed the Xiongnu Cao Hong as great shanyu, and wherever they went ravaged and plundered.
proposals.after: Several tens of thousands of Hu households from Bingzhou, Dingyang and Ercheng rebelled against Hong. They entered Pingyang, attacked General Yao Chengdu, who held the title Liyi, at the Xiongnu fort, and proclaimed Cao Hong of the Xiongnu grand shanyu. Everywhere they went they ravaged and plundered.
proposals.reason: 立義 is an abbreviated general’s title, and 落 counts tribal households or encampments, not tens of thousands of settlements.

proposals.before: Yao Yi marched from Puban, shattered them at Pingyang, sent Cao Hong to Chang'an, and resettled fifteen thousand elite households in Yongzhou.
proposals.after: Yao Yi, General Who Conquers the East, marched from Puban against Cao Hong, routed him at Pingyang, captured him and sent him to Chang’an. Yi resettled fifteen thousand leading households in Yongzhou.
proposals.reason: Restore Yi’s title and the seizure of Cao Hong before he was sent away.

proposals.before: General Who Conquers the East Yao Yi from Puban campaigned against Cao Hong, fought at Pingyang, greatly defeated him, seized Cao Hong, sent him to Chang'an, and moved fifteen thousand notable settlements to Yongzhou.
proposals.after: General Who Conquers the East Yao Yi set out from Puban against Cao Hong. He fought at Pingyang, routed Hong, captured him and sent him to Chang’an. He transferred fifteen thousand of their leading households to Yongzhou.
proposals.reason: 落 counts households or tribal encampments here; the translation inflates their settlement count.

proposals.before: Yang Sheng of Chouqi seized Qishan, captured Wang Zong, and drove on Qinzhou.
proposals.after: Yang Sheng, Duke of Chouchi, stormed Qishan, captured General Wang Zong, who held the title Jianjie, and pressed on toward Qinzhou.
proposals.reason: 仇池 is Chouchi, and 建節 is Wang Zong’s military designation, not part of his name; preserve Sheng’s ducal rank.

proposals.before: Duke of Chouqi Yang Sheng attacked and took Qishan, seized Jianjie Wang Zong, then pressed Qinzhou.
proposals.after: Yang Sheng, Duke of Chouchi, stormed Qishan, captured General Wang Zong, who held the title Jianjie, and pressed on toward Qinzhou.
proposals.reason: 仇池 is Chouchi, and 建節 is Wang Zong’s military designation, not part of his name; preserve Sheng’s ducal rank.

proposals.before: Yao Hong sent Yao Ping; Yang Sheng pulled back.
proposals.after: Yao Hong sent Rear General Yao Ping to relieve Qinzhou, and Yang Sheng withdrew.
proposals.reason: Restore Ping’s rank and mission to relieve Qinzhou.

proposals.before: Yao Song and Yao Ping chased Yang Sheng to Bamboo Ridge while Yao Zan brought Yao Qindu and Wang Huan with palace troops.
proposals.after: Yao Song and Yao Ping pursued Yang Sheng and caught up with him at Bamboo Ridge. Yao Zan hurried to their aid with Yao Qindu, governor of Longxi, Wang Huan, governor of Lüeyang, and the palace guards.
proposals.reason: 及 means actually catching up with Sheng, and the two 太守 are governors of the named commanderies; 禁兵 are palace guards.

proposals.before: Yao Song with Ping pursued Sheng as far as Bamboo Ridge; Yao Zan led Longxi Grand Administrator Yao Qindu and Lüeyang Grand Administrator Wang Huan with household troops to hurry there.
proposals.after: Yao Song and Yao Ping pursued Yang Sheng and caught up with him at Bamboo Ridge. Yao Zan hurried to their aid with Yao Qindu, governor of Longxi, Wang Huan, governor of Lüeyang, and the palace guards.
proposals.reason: 及 means actually catching up with Sheng, and the two 太守 are governors of the named commanderies; 禁兵 are palace guards.

proposals.before: At Qingshui, Yao Zan learned Yao Song had been crushed—Song, Qindu, and Wang Huan all lay dead.
proposals.after: When Yao Zan reached Qingshui, Yang Sheng defeated Yao Song. Song, Yao Qindu and Wang Huan all died in battle.
proposals.reason: The text synchronizes Zan’s arrival and Sheng’s victory; it does not say Zan learned of an earlier event.

proposals.before: Yao Zan reached Qinzhou, then withdrew to Chouqi.
proposals.after: When Yao Zan reached Qinzhou, Yang Sheng withdrew to Chouchi.
proposals.reason: The chapter’s received-text collation identifies missing 盛 before 退還. Chouchi was the domain of Yang Sheng, whose invasion Zan came to relieve (s0055–58). See the Jinshu 119 校勘記, https://skqs.dazhishi.com/show_qmykvqkedv.html .

proposals.before: Zan reached Qinzhou and withdrew to Chouqi.
proposals.after: When Yao Zan reached Qinzhou, Yang Sheng withdrew to Chouchi.
proposals.reason: The chapter’s received-text collation identifies missing 盛 before 退還. Chouchi was the domain of Yang Sheng, whose invasion Zan came to relieve (s0055–58). See the Jinshu 119 校勘記, https://skqs.dazhishi.com/show_qmykvqkedv.html .

proposals.before: Earlier a stone drum in Jixian boomed for hundreds of li and pheasants called without cease.
proposals.after: Earlier a stone drum had sounded in Ji county, Tianshui. It could be heard for several hundred li, and the wild pheasants all crowed.
proposals.reason: The drum was in Ji county of Tianshui, and 皆 means all the pheasants, not uninterrupted calling.

proposals.before: Qinzhou then suffered dozens of quakes, rockslides, and ruined homes—everyone called it an ill omen.
proposals.after: Qinzhou suffered thirty-two earthquakes, eight accompanied by rumbling. Mountains collapsed and houses fell. Everyone took these as ill omens.
proposals.reason: Restore both numbers: thirty-two earthquakes and eight audible rumbles.

proposals.before: Wise men said Qinzhou was Yao Hong's home ground—its ruin foretold his own.
proposals.after: Those who understood the signs thought that, because Qinzhou was Yao Hong’s native place, they foretold his impending downfall.
proposals.reason: The omens concern Hong’s approaching fall because Qinzhou was his home region; the text does not report Qinzhou destroyed.

proposals.before: Those with insight thought Qinzhou was Hong's old homeland—an omen of its about to perish.
proposals.after: Those who understood the signs thought that, because Qinzhou was Yao Hong’s native place, they foretold his impending downfall.
proposals.reason: The omens concern Hong’s approaching fall because Qinzhou was his home region; the text does not report Qinzhou destroyed.

proposals.before: Helian Bobo stormed Yinmi, captured Yao Jundu, and slaughtered over five thousand troops.
proposals.after: Helian Bobo stormed Yinmi, captured Yao Jundu, inspector of Qinzhou, and buried alive more than five thousand officers and men.
proposals.reason: Recover Jundu’s office and the mass burial of the officers and soldiers.

proposals.before: Yao Jundu glared and cursed Bobo's cruelty to his face; Bobo slew him in rage.
proposals.after: Yao Jundu glared at Bobo, loudly denounced his cruelty and refused to submit. Bobo killed him in a rage.
proposals.reason: 不為之屈 explicitly records his refusal to submit.

proposals.before: After Yinmi, Bobo struck toward Yong and drove every northern household toward Five-General Mountain.
proposals.after: After taking Yinmi, Bobo advanced on Yong. The mixed households north of the ridge all fled to Five Generals Mountain.
proposals.reason: 嶺北雜戶 is the specific group of mixed households north of the ridge. They fled as Bobo invaded Yong.

proposals.before: Yao Hui quit Anding with five thousand households for Xinping; Anding men Hu Yan and Hua Tao blocked him, and he galloped alone back to Chang'an.
proposals.after: Yao Hui, General Who Conquers the North, abandoned Anding and fled toward Xinping with five thousand households. Hu Yan, Hua Tao and others from Anding led their followers against him, and Hui returned to Chang’an alone on horseback.
proposals.reason: Restore Hui’s title and Yan and Tao leading followers in resistance.

proposals.before: Mijie Cheng and Pei Qi died fighting Hu Yan; Yao Chen abandoned his post and ran east.
proposals.after: Hu Yan killed the generals Mijie Cheng and Pei Qi, holders of the titles Lijie and Jianwu respectively. Yao Chen, General Who Guards the West, abandoned his garrison and fled east.
proposals.reason: Yan killed the holders of two military titles; dying in battle is unspecified. Chen held the General Who Guards the West title.

proposals.before: Lijie Mijie Cheng and Jianwu Pei Qi were killed by Yan; General Who Guards the West Yao Chen abandoned the garrison and fled east.
proposals.after: Hu Yan killed the generals Mijie Cheng and Pei Qi, holders of the titles Lijie and Jianwu respectively. Yao Chen, General Who Guards the West, abandoned his garrison and fled east.
proposals.reason: Yan killed the holders of two military titles; dying in battle is unspecified. Chen held the General Who Guards the West title.

proposals.before: Yao Shao, Yin Zhao, and Yao Qia led fifty thousand men against Bobo; Yao Hui followed with ten thousand horse.
proposals.after: Yao Shao, General Who Campaigns against the Enemy Yin Zhao, General Who Guards the Army Yao Qia and others led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry against Bobo. Yao Hui followed with ten thousand picked cavalry.
proposals.reason: Restore two military titles, the mixed infantry and cavalry force, and the picked cavalry following them.

proposals.before: At Hengshui Bobo pulled back to Anding; Hu Yan shut the gates, killed thousands of Xianbei, and handed the city over.
proposals.after: Shao’s army halted at Hengshui. Bobo fell back toward Anding to hold it, but Hu Yan shut the gates against him, killed several thousand Xianbei and surrendered the city.
proposals.reason: It is Shao’s army that camps at Hengshui. Bobo’s separate withdrawal was blocked at Anding.

proposals.before: Yao Shao beat Bobo at Ma'an Ridge, chased him toward Zhaona, then broke off the pursuit.
proposals.after: Yao Shao pressed after Bobo, defeated him at Ma’an Slope and pursued him as far as Chaona. Unable to overtake him, Shao returned.
proposals.reason: The pursuit reached 朝那; Shao returned because he failed to catch Bobo.

proposals.before: Shao advanced the army to tread on Bobo, fought at Ma'an Slope, defeated him, pursued to Zhaona, did not catch up and returned.
proposals.after: Yao Shao pressed after Bobo, defeated him at Ma’an Slope and pursued him as far as Chaona. Unable to overtake him, Shao returned.
proposals.reason: The pursuit reached 朝那; Shao returned because he failed to catch Bobo.

proposals.before: Yang Sheng sent his nephew Yang Juan against Changshe.
proposals.after: Yang Sheng sent Yang Juan, his elder brother’s son, to invade Changshe.
proposals.reason: 兄子 specifies the son of Sheng’s elder brother.

proposals.before: The Di chief Gou Ke seized Wuzhangyuan; Yao Wan and Yao Nan marched against him and lost.
proposals.after: Gou Ke, a Di man of Pingyang, gathered more than a thousand men and occupied Wuzhangyuan in revolt. Yao Hong sent Yao Wan, General Who Guards the Distant Lands, and Yao Nan, General Who Restores Might, against him. Gou Ke defeated them.
proposals.reason: Restore Ke’s Pingyang affiliation, force of over a thousand, explicit rebellion and the two generals’ titles. No chieftaincy is stated.

proposals.before: Yao Hong sent Lian Mankui and Yao Guang'er to Chencang; Yang Juan bolted for Sanguan.
proposals.after: Hong sent Lian Manwei, General Who Supports the State, and Forward General Yao Guang’er to attack Yang Juan at Chencang. Juan fled to San Pass.
proposals.reason: 嵬 is Wei in Manwei; both commanders have titles, and their mission was to attack Juan.

proposals.after: Hong sent Lian Manwei, General Who Supports the State, and Forward General Yao Guang’er to attack Yang Juan at Chencang. Juan fled to San Pass.

proposals.before: Bobo's nephew Ti raided Chiyang but Yao Yu, Peng Bailang, and She Xuan threw him back.
proposals.after: Bobo sent Ti, his elder brother’s son, south to invade Chiyang. Yao Yu, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Forward General Peng Bailang, and General She Xuan, who held the title Jianyi, met his attack and drove him back.

proposals.after: Bobo sent Ti, his elder brother’s son, south to invade Chiyang. Yao Yu, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Forward General Peng Bailang, and General She Xuan, who held the title Jianyi, met his attack and drove him back.
proposals.reason: Restore the elder brother’s son, the southward raid and all three officers’ roles; 車騎 denotes a general’s title.

proposals.before: Soon Liu Yu of Jin massed at Pengcheng and sent Tan Daoji and Wang Zhen'e through Huai-Fei against Qiqiu and Xiangcheng while Shen Linzi struck Cangyuan from Bian.
proposals.after: Soon afterward Jin’s grand commandant Liu Yu led a great army against Yao Hong and halted at Pengcheng. He sent Champion General Tan Daoji and Dragon-Soaring General Wang Zhen’e in by the Huai and Fei rivers to attack Qiqiu and Xiangcheng. General Shen Linzi entered the Yellow River from the Bian and attacked Cangyuan.
proposals.reason: Restore Liu Yu’s grand commandant office, his campaign against Hong, his officers’ military titles and Shen Linzi’s route from the Bian into the Yellow River.

proposals.before: Wang Gousheng yielded Qiqiu to Wang Zhen'e, Yao Zhang yielded Xiangcheng to Tan Daoji, and the Jin host poured through Yingkou almost unopposed.
proposals.after: Hong’s general Wang Gousheng surrendered Qiqiu to Wang Zhen’e, and Yao Zhang, inspector of Xuzhou, surrendered Xiangcheng to Tan Daoji. The Jin army then entered Yingkou, and many places submitted as it advanced.
proposals.reason: 多 qualifies submissions: many places submitted. The first officer is Hong’s general and the second inspector of Xuzhou.

proposals.before: Hong's general Wang Gousheng surrendered Qiqiu to Zhen'e; Xuzhou Inspector Yao Zhang surrendered Xiangcheng to Daoji; the royal army then entered Yingkou, and wherever it went there was surrender.
proposals.after: Hong’s general Wang Gousheng surrendered Qiqiu to Wang Zhen’e, and Yao Zhang, inspector of Xuzhou, surrendered Xiangcheng to Tan Daoji. The Jin army then entered Yingkou, and many places submitted as it advanced.
proposals.reason: 多 qualifies submissions: many places submitted. The first officer is Hong’s general and the second inspector of Xuzhou.

proposals.before: Only Dong Zun of Xin'cai held out until Tan Daoji stormed the city and bound him before the camp.
proposals.after: Only Dong Zun, governor of Xincai, held firm and refused to surrender. Tan Daoji stormed the place, had Zun bound and brought him to the gate of the camp.
proposals.reason: Restore Dong’s governorship and being brought bound to the camp gate.

proposals.before: Dong Zun snapped: "Ancient kings campaigned with courtesy toward worthy foes.
proposals.after: With a stern expression Dong Zun said, “When kings of old made war on other states, they treated men of worth with courtesy.
proposals.reason: 士 means men of standing or worth here; neither enemies specifically nor knights as a military class.

proposals.before: Zun in stern color said, "Kings of old in campaigning against states treated knights with ritual.
proposals.after: With a stern expression Dong Zun said, “When kings of old made war on other states, they treated men of worth with courtesy.
proposals.reason: 士 means men of standing or worth here; neither enemies specifically nor knights as a military class.

proposals.before: How dare you wage an unjust war and dishonor a loyal governor?"
proposals.after: How can you wage war unjustly and treat a man of distinction in another state with such discourtesy?”

proposals.before: How can you, sir, march with unrighteous conduct and treat a state's knights without ritual."

proposals.before: Yao Shao raced back to warn Yao Hong: "Jin is past Xuchang—Yuzhou and Anding are too far to save. Move frontier households into the capital for a hundred thousand veterans.
proposals.after: When Yao Shao heard of the Jin army’s arrival, he returned to Chang’an and told Hong, “Jin has already passed Xuchang. Yuzhou and Anding are isolated and distant and would be hard to relieve in an emergency. Move the garrison households inward to strengthen the capital region. We could raise a hundred thousand picked troops, enough to go anywhere in the realm.
proposals.reason: Restore Chang’an, Shao’s reason for returning, the garrisons’ isolation, and the claim the resulting force could range across the realm.

proposals.before: Liang Xi argued: "Yao Hui terrifies the north; his garrisons hate Bobo and will die before yielding—Bobo cannot skip Anding to strike the core.
proposals.after: Liang Xi, the left vice-director, said, “Yao Hui, Duke of Qi, is brave and has a formidable reputation. The people north of the ridge fear him. The garrison’s people already bear Bobo a deep grudge and should hold out to the death without wavering. Bobo cannot bypass Anding and raid the distant capital region.
proposals.reason: Restore Liang’s office, Hui’s ducal rank, martial reputation north of the ridge, and the residents’ own hostility and determination.

proposals.before: Personnel clerk Yi Heng whispered: "Yao Hui saved you at Guangping yet has never been richly rewarded.
proposals.after: Yi Heng, a gentleman of the Personnel Department, privately told Hong, “Yao Hui, Duke of Qi, rendered Your Majesty loyal service in the crisis over the Duke of Guangping. Since you took the throne, he has received no special reward in recognition of his devotion.
proposals.reason: 廣平之難 refers to the crisis over Yao Bi, Duke of Guangping (Jinshu 118), not a rescue at a town. Restore the accession, Hui’s rank and Heng’s office.

proposals.before: Personnel Director Yi Heng secretly said to Hong, "Duke of Qi Hui at the Guangping crisis had loyal merit toward Your Majesty; since Your Majesty's dragon flight and succession, there has been no special reward to answer his intent.
proposals.after: Yi Heng, a gentleman of the Personnel Department, privately told Hong, “Yao Hui, Duke of Qi, rendered Your Majesty loyal service in the crisis over the Duke of Guangping. Since you took the throne, he has received no special reward in recognition of his devotion.
proposals.reason: 廣平之難 refers to the crisis over Yao Bi, Duke of Guangping (Jinshu 118), not a rescue at a town. Restore the accession, Hui’s rank and Heng’s office.

proposals.before: When Jin reached Chenggao, Yao Guang in Luoyang begged for reinforcements.
proposals.after: When the Jin army reached Chenggao, Yao Guang, General Who Conquers the South, was garrisoning Luoyang. He sent a rider at speed to request relief.
proposals.reason: Restore Guang’s military title, the Luoyang garrison and his urgent mounted messenger.

proposals.before: Yao Hong sent Yan Sheng with three thousand horse, Yao Yinan with ten thousand foot to Luoyang, and Yao Yi to Shan ford as a screen.
proposals.after: Hong sent Yan Sheng, colonel of the Yue Cavalry, with three thousand horsemen to the rescue and the Martial Guard commander Yao Yinan with ten thousand infantry to help defend Luoyang. He also sent Yao Yi, General Who Conquers the East and governor of Bingzhou, south to camp at Shan Ford in support.
proposals.reason: The officers have distinct titles, Yi was ordered south to camp at Shan Ford, and his force was to support the relief effort.

proposals.before: Zhao Xuan warned Yao Guang: "The enemy is on top of us, the people panic, and we are outnumbered.
proposals.after: Guang’s subordinate commander Zhao Xuan urged him, “The invaders have already penetrated deep into our territory. The people are terrified, and our forces are so outnumbered that it will be hard to meet the enemy.
proposals.reason: Restore Xuan’s relationship to Guang, the depth of the incursion and the difficulty of meeting the enemy.

proposals.before: Hold that fortress and Jin will never dare push west of it.
proposals.after: With Jinyong strongly held and our army intact, the invaders from Wu will never dare pass the fortress and march west.
proposals.reason: Restore the army’s preservation and Zhao’s designation of the southern invaders.

proposals.before: Starve them under your walls without lifting another spear."
proposals.after: Keep them pinned beneath strong walls, and you can wait and take advantage of their exhaustion.”
proposals.reason: 困 means pinning or wearing down the enemy. The text does not specify starving them.

proposals.before: Yao Guang listened: he sent Zhao Xuan to Bai Valley and Shi Wuhui to Gong to block Jin.
proposals.after: Guang took their advice and sent Zhao Xuan south with over a thousand picked troops to defend the Baigu stockade, and General Shi Wuhui, holder of the title Guangwu, east to garrison Gongcheng and bar the Jin army.
proposals.reason: Restore the thousand-plus picked troops, the directions and Guangwu as a general’s title.

proposals.before: Guang followed them, then sent Xuan leading more than a thousand picked troops south to guard the Bai Valley stockade, Guangwu Shi Wuhui east to guard Gong city, to block the royal army.
proposals.after: Guang took their advice and sent Zhao Xuan south with over a thousand picked troops to defend the Baigu stockade, and General Shi Wuhui, holder of the title Guangwu, east to garrison Gongcheng and bar the Jin army.
proposals.reason: Restore the thousand-plus picked troops, the directions and Guangwu as a general’s title.

proposals.before: Xuan wept and said to Guang, "Xuan has received triple favor from three emperors—what I hold is only death.
proposals.after: Xuan wept and said to Guang, “Three emperors have shown me great favor. All I can do is die at my post.
proposals.reason: 重恩 means great favor, not triple favor. 正死 concerns dying at his post.

proposals.before: Yangcheng, Chenggao, Xingyang, and Wulao fell; Tan Daoji rolled forward unchecked.
proposals.after: Meanwhile Yangcheng, Chenggao, Xingyang and Wulao all surrendered, and Tan Daoji and the others advanced swiftly without a check.
proposals.reason: 悉降 means all four cities surrendered; restore Daoji’s companions.

proposals.before: Zhao Xuan fought Mao Dezu at Baigu, was overrun and cut down; Qian Jian tried to drag him clear but Zhao said, "I am finished—save yourself."
proposals.after: At Baigu, Zhao Xuan fought the Jin general Mao Dezu and was defeated by superior numbers. He received more than ten wounds and cried out from the ground. His major, Qian Jian, braved the blades to hold him in his arms and wept. Xuan said, “My wounds are grave. You must leave at once.”
proposals.reason: The English omits numerical inferiority, more than ten wounds, the cry and Jian’s tears, and inserts an attempt to drag Xuan away.

proposals.before: Qian Jian said, "If you fall, I fall with you."
proposals.after: Qian Jian replied, “If you do not survive, General, I will die with you. If I left, where would I go?”
proposals.reason: Restore Jian’s rhetorical refusal to leave.

proposals.before: Yan Sheng and Yao Yinan stopped cold when they heard Luoyang was lost.
proposals.after: Yan Sheng had reached Xin’an and Yao Yinan had reached Hucheng. Luoyang had already fallen, so they stayed in camp and advanced no farther.
proposals.reason: Restore each officer’s location and the decision to remain in camp without advancing.

proposals.before: Prince Yao Yi was vain and credulous; Sun Chang urged him to strike Chang'an, kill Yao Shao, and seize the throne.
proposals.after: Yao Yi was mean and treacherous and easily misled by those he trusted. His major Sun Chang, a cunning flatterer who delighted in turmoil and misfortune, urged him to raid Chang’an, kill Yao Shao, depose Yao Hong and set himself on the throne.
proposals.reason: Restore Yi’s mean and treacherous disposition, Sun Chang’s staff office and delight in trouble, and the explicit deposition of Hong.

proposals.before: Yao Yi marched to Shan ford and scattered state grain to buy tribal loyalty.
proposals.after: Yi took his advice and led troops to Shan Ford. He distributed grain to the non-Chinese and Chinese inhabitants north of the Yellow River, intending to deplete the state reserves, attract the Qiang groups of Herong and win personal credit for the largesse.
proposals.reason: 河北 is north of the Yellow River. Yi distributes to both indigenous and Chinese people and seeks separately to drain state reserves, draw in the Herong Qiang and cultivate personal favor.

proposals.before: Yi accepted it, then led troops to Shan ford, scattered grain to give to Hebei Yi and Xia of every sort, wishing to hollow out state stores, summon and win the peace-with-barbarians Qiang, and plant private favor.
proposals.after: Yi took his advice and led troops to Shan Ford. He distributed grain to the non-Chinese and Chinese inhabitants north of the Yellow River, intending to deplete the state reserves, attract the Qiang groups of Herong and win personal credit for the largesse.

proposals.before: Zhang Chang and Zuo Ya warned: "You are the emperor's uncle on the western front—your fate is the dynasty's fate.
proposals.after: Yi’s Left Regular Attendant Zhang Chang and Attendant Gentleman Zuo Ya earnestly remonstrated with him: “Your Highness is the emperor’s younger brother by the same mother. You bear the weight of regional command and share the state’s safety and danger, its joys and its sorrows.

proposals.before: Yi's left constant attendant Zhang Chang and attendant Zuo Ya firmly remonstrated Yi, saying, "Your Highness, with the closeness of mother's-brother kin, holds the weight of dividing Shaan; safety and peril, rest and sorrow, you share with the state.

proposals.before: Grain is the root of power, and you are pouring it away.
proposals.after: Grain is the foundation of the state, yet you are giving it away.
proposals.reason: 國 is the state whose stores Yi is depleting.

proposals.before: Yao Yi had them beaten to death.
proposals.after: In anger, Yao Yi had the two men flogged and killed.
proposals.reason: 怒 gives Yi’s reaction to their remonstrance.

proposals.before: Yao Hong called Yao Shao into the palace for a secret council.
proposals.after: When Yao Hong heard of this, he summoned Yao Shao and others to deliberate in secret in the court hall.
proposals.reason: Restore Hong’s hearing the report, the other summoned advisers and the court hall.

proposals.before: Yao Shao said: "Yao Yi is weak-minded; Sun Chang made him do this.
proposals.after: Yao Shao said, “Yi is narrow in outlook and easily swayed by others. Sun Chang must be the one behind this affair.
proposals.reason: Shao explains Yi’s limited judgment and susceptibility to influence; Sun Chang’s authorship is an inference.

proposals.before: Arrest Sun Chang, put Yao Zan in Shan, and I will take Tong Pass—if they obey, Yao Yi can still march east against Jin.
proposals.after: Just send a swift rider to summon Sun Chang, and send Pacifying General Yao Zan to hold the city of Shan. I will go to Tong Pass to direct the armies. If Chang comes in obedience to the edict, I will have Yi lead the troops now available in Hedong to join us against the invaders from Wu.
proposals.reason: 征暢 summons Chang; it does not order his arrest. He is to comply with the edict, and Yi would lead the existing troops of Hedong alongside Shao against the southern invaders.

proposals.before: Only dispatch riders at speed to summon Chang; send General Who Pacifies Zan to hold Shan city; I will go to Tong Pass to command all armies—if Chang comes bearing the edict, I will order Yi to lead Hedong's available troops together to pacify the Wu bandit.
proposals.after: Just send a swift rider to summon Sun Chang, and send Pacifying General Yao Zan to hold the city of Shan. I will go to Tong Pass to direct the armies. proposals.before: If they defy the edict, publish their treason and attack."
proposals.after: If rebellion is already under way and they resist the edict, we should proclaim their crime to the realm and sound the drums to attack them.”
proposals.reason: Shao makes the plan conditional on an established breach and resistance to the edict, and directs sounding the attack drums.

proposals.before: He sent Yao Zan, Simo Guofan, and She Xuan to Shan and Yao Lü to Tong Pass.
proposals.after: Hong sent Yao Zan, Champion General Sima Guofan and General She Xuan, holder of the title Jianyi, to encamp at Shan Ford, and Martial Guard commander Yao Lü to encamp at Tong Pass.

proposals.before: Thereupon he sent Yao Zan and champion major Simo Guofan, Jianyi She Xuan to camp at Shan ford, Martial Guard Yao Lü to camp at Tong Pass.
proposals.after: Hong sent Yao Zan, Champion General Sima Guofan and General She Xuan, holder of the title Jianyi, to encamp at Shan Ford, and Martial Guard commander Yao Lü to encamp at Tong Pass.
